title: Failover: integration tests for rollback + hold-down timers (CI wiring + flaky triage)
author: Jordan Lee
body:
Context: As part of the regional failover automation upgrade, we rely on (a) hold-down timers to prevent flappy failovers and (b) rollback to unwind progressive failover safely when the source region recovers or when safe-to-failover checks fail mid-flight. We had decent unit coverage for the trigger module + state machine transitions, but we were missing end-to-end coverage across the orchestrator, policy store wiring, and time-based hysteresis/hold-down behavior.

This PR adds an integration test suite that runs against the orchestrator in-process with a fake routing policy store and a controllable clock, validating the following scenarios:
- Rollback from an in-progress progressive failover (25% -> 50% -> rollback to 0%) preserves invariants: no customer tier scope expansion during rollback, audit log entries for each transition, and policy store ends in a consistent "primary region" state.
- Hold-down timers prevent immediate re-failover: after a rollback or recovery transition, the orchestrator should ignore subsequent degrade signals for the configured hold-down window unless a "hard fail" signal persists past the emergency threshold.
- Manual override precedence: manual "freeze" blocks automatic transitions, and removing the freeze does not retroactively apply queued actions; it resumes evaluation from current region health snapshot.
- Stop condition behavior: if safe-to-failover capacity checks fail in the target region, the orchestrator should halt at current stage and automatically roll back if the stage exceeded the configured "max_canary_percent_without_capacity_confirmation".

Implementation details:
- Introduces a test-only FakeClock (monotonic) and routes orchestrator timers through the injected clock to make hold-down behavior deterministic (no sleep-based tests).
- Adds a minimal "routing-policy-sandbox" implementation to validate policy write semantics (CAS failures, version increments, and idempotent writes) without needing a real Redis/etcd dependency.
- Adds golden audit assertions: we assert on stable fields only (event type, from/to state, reason code, guard decisions, and correlation_id) to avoid brittle comparisons.

CI changes + flaky triage notes:
- New CI job "failover-integration" running under the existing integration runner pool with an explicit CPU quota (some flakes were traced to timeouts under contention).
- Marks 2 existing routing integration tests as "quarantined" (still run nightly) because they rely on wall-clock sleeps and were intermittently failing when the runner is noisy; follow-up filed in ENG-2853 to refactor those onto FakeClock as well.
- Adds a retry-once for the new failover-integration job only when the failure signature matches known infra flakes (gRPC connection reset during container startup). Non-infra failures still fail fast.

Notes:
- These tests assume the orchestrator is running with feature flags that enable progressive failover + hold-down timers. They do not validate DNS/edge propagation behavior; those remain covered by terraform plan checks + game day procedures.
- The suite runs in ~6m locally and ~8–10m in CI. If this becomes a bottleneck we can split into "fast" (state machine + policy store) and "slow" (multi-step progressive scenarios).

Release impact:
- No production behavior changes. Test + CI only.

Related:
- ENG-2844 (trigger evaluation/state machine)
- ENG-2846 (progressive failover)
- ENG-2853 (post-rollout retro + tuning; includes test debt cleanup)
- PRs: 98248 (state machine + audit), 98277 (progressive failover), 98305 (safe-to-failover checks)

Verification:
- Ran full test suite locally (pass)
- Ran new failover-integration job 10x locally with random seed variations (pass)
- Observed one CI failure due to runner startup reset; addressed via targeted retry and increasing startup readiness timeout from 20s -> 45s.
commits: test(failover): add integration harness w/ FakeClock + sandbox policy store
test(failover): rollback scenarios + hold-down timer assertions
test(failover): manual override precedence + stop condition coverage
ci: add failover-integration workflow + runner resource caps
ci: quarantine two sleep-based routing integration tests (nightly only)

review_conversation: Miles Thornton (requested changes, 2025-04-24): The hold-down test looks good, but we're asserting on the full audit payload (including timestamps). Can we avoid brittleness by checking stable fields + reason codes only? Also, can we add a case where we rollback while a new degrade signal is present (should still respect hold-down).
Jordan Lee (author, 2025-04-24): Good call. Updated audit assertions to use a stable subset + added a new test "rollback_then_degrade_ignored_during_holddown" advancing FakeClock across the window.
Benji Okafor (comment, 2025-04-25): For the CAS failure path: can we ensure we don't spin on retries under contention? We had an incident in another component where a tight loop created noisy logs.

Jordan Lee (author, 2025-04-25): Added bounded retries (max 3) with jittered backoff in the sandbox store and an assertion that we surface an error if CAS keeps failing. Also reduced log level for expected CAS contention in test harness.

Elena Popov (requested changes, 2025-04-26): CI wiring: the new job is good, but please avoid global retry logic. Keep retry scoped to known infra flakes and add a pointer in docs/ci/flaky-tests.md so oncall knows what to do when it fails.

Jordan Lee (author, 2025-04-26): Done. Retry is now conditional on the known startup reset signature; otherwise fail fast. Added a small section to docs/ci/flaky-tests.md with runbook steps (rerun job, check runner health).

Connor O'Brien (approval, 2025-04-29): Looked through the workflow changes and quarantining. +1. Please file the follow-up to refactor the quarantined tests onto FakeClock if it isn't already tracked.
Jordan Lee (author, 2025-04-29): Follow-up is tracked under ENG-2853 as a subtask. Thanks.
Miles Thornton (approval, 2025-04-29): LGTM. This closes a gap we called out in the game day retro.
